lessons.commonMistake: After does or doesn’t, drop the -s: Does she work?
lessons.diagramCaption: An action that repeats over time

examples.sentence: I walk to work every day.

exercises.explanation: A daily routine uses Present Simple.
exercises.prompt: I ___ to school by bus every day.

lessons.form: I/you/we/they + verb · he/she/it + verb-s. For questions and negatives, use do or does + base verb.

mistake.why: After does or doesn’t the verb loses its -s.

lessons.summary: Habits and things that are generally true
lessons.title: Present Simple
lessons.use: Use it for routines, facts, and regular actions.

lessons.commonMistake: Use Present Simple for routines: I read every evening.
lessons.diagramCaption: An action in progress now

examples.sentence: They’re staying with friends this week.

lessons.form: am/is/are + verb-ing. For questions, put am/is/are before the subject.

mistake.why: Routines use Present Simple, not Present Continuous.

lessons.summary: Something happening now or around now
lessons.title: Present Continuous
lessons.use: Use it for an action in progress now or a temporary situation.

lessons.commonMistake: After did or didn’t, use the base verb: She didn’t go.
lessons.diagramCaption: A finished point before now

examples.meaning: Finished at a known past time

exercises.explanation: Finished time (last year): Past Simple, and go is irregular.
Past questions use did + base verb.

lessons.form: Regular verbs: verb-ed. Irregular verbs: past form. Questions and negatives: did + base verb.

mistake.why: After did or didn’t, use the base verb.

lessons.summary: A finished action at a past time
lessons.title: Past Simple
lessons.use: Use it when an event is complete and its time is in the past.

lessons.commonMistake: The shorter interrupting action often uses Past Simple.
lessons.diagramCaption: A stretch of time before now

examples.meaning: The cooking was already in progress
examples.sentence: I was cooking when you called.

examples.meaning: In progress at a past time

exercises.explanation: An action in progress at a past moment: was/were + verb-ing.
exercises.prompt: At 8 o’clock last night, I ___ TV.

exercises.explanation: The longer action in progress uses Past Continuous; the short event uses Past Simple.

exercises.prompt: They ___ football when it started to rain.

lessons.form: was/were + verb-ing.

mistake.right: I was walking home when I saw an accident.
mistake.why: The shorter interrupting action usually uses Past Simple.
mistake.wrong: I was walking home when I was seeing an accident.

lessons.summary: An action in progress in the past
lessons.title: Past Continuous
lessons.use: Use it for background activity or an action interrupted by another event.

lessons.commonMistake: After will and going to, use the base verb.
lessons.diagramCaption: An event after now

exercises.prompt: Look at those clouds. It ___ rain.

exercises.explanation: A decision made at the moment of speaking: will.
exercises.prompt: I’m cold. I ___ close the window.

exercises.explanation: A plan already made: be going to or present continuous.
exercises.prompt: We ___ to Spain next month. We’ve booked the flights.

lessons.form: will + base verb · am/is/are going to + base verb · am/is/are + verb-ing.

mistake.why: After will and going to, use the base verb.

lessons.summary: Will, going to, and present arrangements
lessons.title: Talking about the future
lessons.use: Choose will for a decision made now or a prediction; going to for a plan or visible evidence; Present Continuous for a fixed arrangement.

lessons.commonMistake: With a finished time such as yesterday, use Past Simple: I lost them yesterday.
lessons.diagramCaption: Something in the past with a link to now

exercises.explanation: Since + a starting point needs Present Perfect.

lessons.form: have/has + past participle.

mistake.why: A finished time such as yesterday needs Past Simple.

lessons.summary: A past action connected to now
lessons.title: Present Perfect
lessons.use: Use it for experience or a past action whose result matters now. The exact past time is not stated.

lessons.commonMistake: Use for with a duration and since with a starting point, not the reverse.
lessons.diagramCaption: Activity over time with a present connection

examples.meaning: The activity began earlier and continues
examples.sentence: I’ve been studying for two hours.
She’s been painting; her hands are blue.

exercises.explanation: Activity that continued up to now: have/has been + verb-ing.
How long + have you been + verb-ing.
For + period with an activity continuing now.

lessons.form: have/has been + verb-ing; often with for or since.

mistake.right: I’ve been waiting for two hours.
mistake.why: Use for with a duration and since with a starting point.
mistake.wrong: I’ve been waiting since two hours.

lessons.summary: An activity continuing up to now
lessons.title: Present Perfect Continuous
lessons.use: Use it to stress the duration or recent activity behind a present result.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not use would for a former state: I would live there is not the same as I used to live there.
lessons.diagramCaption: Used to and would have different ranges of meaning

examples.sentence: I used to live by the sea.
Every summer, we would swim at dawn.

exercises.explanation: would + base verb for repeated past actions.
exercises.prompt: When I was a child, I ___ play outside every day.

exercises.explanation: used to + base verb for a past state.
exercises.prompt: We ___ live in a small village.

exercises.explanation: A past habit that no longer continues.

lessons.form: used to + base verb · would + base verb · past simple.

mistake.right: I used to live in Rome when I was young.
mistake.why: Would cannot describe a former state; use used to.
mistake.wrong: I would live in Rome when I was young.

lessons.summary: Used to, would, and past routines
lessons.title: Past habits
lessons.use: Use used to for past habits or states that are no longer true. Would can describe repeated past actions, but usually not past states.

lessons.commonMistake: Don’t use Present Perfect with a finished time: say I saw him yesterday, not I have seen him yesterday.
lessons.diagramCaption: Finished time or link to the present

examples.sentence: I saw that film last week.

exercises.explanation: Yesterday is a finished time: Past Simple.
The result matters now: Present Perfect.
exercises.prompt: I ___ my phone. Can you help me look?

exercises.explanation: Life experience, no time given: Have you ever…?
In 2019 is a finished time: Past Simple.

lessons.form: Past Simple: I lost my keys yesterday. Present Perfect: I have lost my keys (I still can’t find them).

mistake.why: A finished time word needs Past Simple.

lessons.summary: Connected to now, or finished and over
lessons.title: Present Perfect or Past Simple?
lessons.use: Use Past Simple for a finished time (yesterday, in 2019, last week). Use Present Perfect when the time is not given or the result matters now.

lessons.commonMistake: Don’t mix them: I have known her since three years is wrong. Say for three years.
lessons.diagramCaption: Three ways to talk about time

examples.sentence: I’ve lived here for five years.
I moved here five years ago.

exercises.explanation: Ten years is a length of time: for.
Monday is a starting point: since.

lessons.form: for + period (for two years) · since + point (since 2022) · period + ago (two years ago, with Past Simple).

mistake.right: I have known her for three years.
mistake.why: Use for with a length of time and since with a starting point.
mistake.wrong: I have known her since three years.

lessons.summary: Length of time, starting point, and time back from now
lessons.title: For, Since and Ago
lessons.use: Use for with a length of time, since with a starting point, and ago with a past time counted back from now.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not use had with a past form: had went is wrong; had gone is right.
lessons.diagramCaption: One past action precedes another

examples.sentence: The train had left when we arrived.
I had never flown before that trip.

exercises.explanation: The earlier past action uses had + past participle.
The loss happened before she was sad.
exercises.prompt: She was sad because she ___ her keys.
He ___ never seen snow before he moved to Canada.

lessons.form: had + past participle.

mistake.why: Had is followed by the past participle, not the Past Simple form.

lessons.summary: The earlier of two past events
lessons.title: Past Perfect Simple
lessons.use: Use it to make clear that one past event happened before another.

lessons.commonMistake: Use had been, not have been, when both reference points are in the past.
lessons.diagramCaption: Ongoing activity before another past event

examples.sentence: We had been walking for hours when it rained.

examples.meaning: Earlier activity explains a past result
examples.sentence: Her eyes were tired because she had been reading.

exercises.explanation: had been + verb-ing for an activity before a past moment.
exercises.prompt: She was tired because she ___ for hours.

exercises.explanation: Waiting continued up to a past moment.
exercises.prompt: They ___ for an hour when the bus finally came.

exercises.explanation: Past evidence of an earlier activity.

lessons.form: had been + verb-ing.

mistake.right: When I arrived, they had been waiting for an hour.
mistake.why: Use had been when both points are in the past.
mistake.wrong: When I arrived, they have been waiting for an hour.

lessons.title: Past Perfect Continuous
lessons.use: Use it to show how long an activity had been continuing before another past event.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not leave out be: will working is wrong.
lessons.diagramCaption: A future point inside an ongoing action

examples.meaning: Work will be in progress then

examples.sentence: This time tomorrow, we’ll be flying.

exercises.explanation: will be + verb-ing for an action in progress in the future.
exercises.prompt: This time tomorrow, I ___ on a beach.

exercises.explanation: Action in progress at a future time.

exercises.prompt: ___ you be using the car tonight?

lessons.form: will be + verb-ing.

mistake.right: This time tomorrow I will be working.
mistake.why: Will be is needed before the -ing form.
mistake.wrong: This time tomorrow I will working.

lessons.summary: In progress at a future time
lessons.title: Future Continuous
lessons.use: Use it for an activity expected to be underway at a specified future moment.

lessons.commonMistake: After will have, use the past participle: will have written.
lessons.diagramCaption: Completion comes before a future deadline

examples.sentence: By Friday, I’ll have finished the report.
They’ll have left by the time we arrive.

exercises.explanation: will have + past participle: done before a future time.
will have been shows duration up to a future time.
exercises.prompt: They ___ married for ten years next June.

lessons.form: will have + past participle; often with by.

mistake.right: By June I will have written it.
mistake.why: After will have, use the past participle.
mistake.wrong: By June I will have wrote it.

lessons.title: Future Perfect
lessons.use: Use it to say an action will be complete by a future deadline.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not add will to the if-clause for a general fact.
lessons.diagramCaption: A general condition leads to a general result

examples.sentence: If I skip breakfast, I get hungry early.
When ice warms up, it melts.

exercises.explanation: General truths use if + present, present.

exercises.prompt: If I ___ coffee late, I can’t sleep.
Water ___ if the temperature falls below zero.

lessons.form: If + present simple, present simple. When can replace if for a predictable result.

mistake.right: If you heat ice, it melts.
mistake.why: A general fact uses the present in both parts.
mistake.wrong: If you heat ice, it will melt.

lessons.title: Zero Conditional
lessons.use: Use it for general facts, instructions, and repeated results.

lessons.commonMistake: Use present, not will, after if: If it rains, we’ll stay in.
lessons.diagramCaption: A realistic condition points to a future result

examples.sentence: If the bus is late, I’ll walk.

examples.meaning: Unless = if it does not rain
examples.sentence: We’ll go outside unless it rains.

exercises.prompt: If it rains, we ___ at home.

exercises.explanation: No will after if in the condition part.
exercises.prompt: If you ___ hard, you will pass.
She will call you if she ___ time.
If he ___ late, we’ll start without him.

lessons.form: If + present simple, will + base verb. The clauses can change order; add a comma when if comes first.

mistake.right: If it rains, we’ll stay in.
mistake.why: Use the present, not will, after if.
mistake.wrong: If it will rain, we’ll stay in.

lessons.title: First Conditional
lessons.use: Use it for a possible future condition and its likely result. Unless means if not.

lessons.commonMistake: Past form here expresses distance from reality, not necessarily past time.
lessons.diagramCaption: An unreal or unlikely condition creates an imagined result

examples.meaning: I do not have enough time now
examples.sentence: If I had more time, I’d learn Italian.
If she were here, she would know what to do.

exercises.prompt: If I ___ rich, I would travel.

exercises.explanation: would + base verb in the result.

exercises.prompt: What ___ you do if you won?

lessons.form: If + past simple, would + base verb. Were is common with I/he/she/it in careful style.

mistake.why: The past form in the if-part shows an unreal situation.
mistake.wrong: If I would win, I’d travel.

lessons.title: Second Conditional
lessons.use: Use it for a situation that is unlikely or not true now and imagine its result.

lessons.commonMistake: Keep would out of the if-clause: If I had known, not if I would have known.
lessons.diagramCaption: Both the condition and result are imagined in the past

examples.meaning: We left late and missed it
examples.sentence: If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train.
She would have joined us if she had known.

exercises.explanation: if + past perfect, would have + past participle.
exercises.prompt: If I ___ harder, I would have passed.

exercises.explanation: Past unreal condition: had + past participle.
exercises.prompt: She would have come if she ___ about it.

exercises.explanation: would have + past participle for the imagined result.
exercises.prompt: If we had left earlier, we ___ the train.

lessons.form: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

mistake.right: If I had known, I would have called.
mistake.why: Keep would out of the if-clause.
mistake.wrong: If I would have known, I would have called.

lessons.summary: An alternative to a finished past
lessons.title: Third Conditional
lessons.use: Use it to imagine how a past result could have changed.

lessons.commonMistake: Choose each verb form by its own time reference; do not force both clauses into the same time.
lessons.diagramCaption: The two clauses can refer to different times

examples.sentence: If I had slept more, I wouldn’t be tired now.
If she spoke French, she would have taken that job.

exercises.explanation: Past condition, present result: would + base verb.
exercises.prompt: If I had taken that job, I ___ in London now.

exercises.explanation: A general present quality (were) with a past result.
exercises.prompt: If she ___ more careful, she wouldn’t have broken it.

exercises.explanation: Past condition, present result: would + base verb.
exercises.prompt: If I had studied medicine, I ___ a doctor now.

lessons.form: If + past perfect, would + base verb for a present result; if + past simple, would have + participle for a past result.

mistake.right: If I had taken the job, I would live in London now.
mistake.why: Choose each verb form by its own time reference.
mistake.wrong: If I had taken the job, I would have lived in London now.

lessons.summary: A past cause with a present result, or the reverse
lessons.title: Mixed Conditionals
lessons.use: Use mixed forms when the imagined condition and result belong to different times.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not use wish + would for your own deliberate action: say I wish I could leave.
lessons.diagramCaption: Verb form shows whether the wish concerns now, the past, or change

examples.meaning: I do not know it now
examples.sentence: I wish I knew the answer.
If only we had booked earlier.

examples.meaning: I want the situation to change
examples.sentence: I wish the noise would stop.

exercises.explanation: A present wish uses the past form.
exercises.prompt: I wish I ___ more free time.

exercises.explanation: A past regret uses had + past participle.
exercises.prompt: I wish I ___ the answer yesterday.

exercises.explanation: wish/if only + would for annoying things we want to change.

lessons.form: wish + past simple · wish + past perfect · wish + would + base verb.

mistake.right: I wish I could leave early.
mistake.why: Wish + would is for other people or things, not your own choice.
mistake.wrong: I wish I would leave early.

lessons.title: Wish and if only
lessons.use: Use a past form for a present wish, past perfect for a past regret, and would for a change you want another person or situation to make.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not add to after can or could: can swim, not can to swim.
lessons.diagramCaption: Different forms express ability and permission

exercises.explanation: couldn’t is the past of can’t for general ability.
exercises.prompt: When I was five, I ___ swim.

lessons.form: can/could + base verb · be able to + base verb.

mistake.why: No to after can or could.

lessons.summary: Can, could, and be able to
lessons.title: Ability and permission
lessons.use: Use can for present ability or informal permission; could can describe general past ability or make a polite request.

lessons.commonMistake: Mustn’t means forbidden; don’t have to means optional.
lessons.diagramCaption: Prohibition and lack of necessity are different

examples.sentence: You must wear a helmet here.
You don’t have to come early.

exercises.prompt: You ___ wear a seatbelt. It’s the law.
You ___ see a doctor. You look ill.
You ___ come early. We start late.

lessons.form: modal + base verb · have to + base verb.

mistake.right: You mustn’t park here. It’s forbidden.
mistake.why: Mustn’t means forbidden; don’t have to means not necessary.
mistake.wrong: You don’t have to park here. It’s forbidden.

lessons.summary: Must, have to, mustn’t, and should
lessons.title: Obligation, prohibition, and advice
lessons.use: Use must/have to for necessity, mustn’t for prohibition, don’t have to for no necessity, and should for advice.

lessons.commonMistake: Would you like to help? asks about willingness; Shall I help? offers your help.
lessons.diagramCaption: The subject and modal show who will act

exercises.explanation: Could you…? is a polite request.

exercises.prompt: ___ I help you with your bags?

lessons.form: Could you + base verb? · Would you like + noun/to-infinitive? · Shall I + base verb?

mistake.why: Shall I offers help; would you like asks about willingness.

lessons.title: Requests and offers
lessons.use: Choose a modal to make a request, offer help, or ask permission with the right degree of politeness.

lessons.commonMistake: Mustn’t expresses prohibition, not a negative deduction; use can’t be.
lessons.diagramCaption: Modal choice reflects the strength of evidence

examples.sentence: She might be at the library.
The lights are on; they must be home.
He can’t be asleep; I can hear him talking.

exercises.prompt: He’s not answering. He ___ be asleep.

exercises.explanation: can’t = sure it is not true.

exercises.prompt: She ___ be at home, but I’m not sure.

lessons.form: modal + base verb; for an action happening now, modal + be + verb-ing.

mistake.right: He can’t be at home. The lights are off.
mistake.why: Mustn’t is prohibition; can’t is a negative deduction.
mistake.wrong: He mustn’t be at home. The lights are off.

lessons.title: Possibility and deduction
lessons.use: Use might/may/could for possibility, must for a strong positive deduction, and can’t for a strong negative one.

lessons.commonMistake: Don’t add to or -s: She might comes is wrong. Say She might come.
lessons.diagramCaption: From certain to possible

examples.sentence: She may have missed the bus.

exercises.prompt: Take a coat. It ___ rain later.

exercises.explanation: may has no -s and no to.
exercises.prompt: I’m not sure. She ___ come tonight.

lessons.form: may / might + base verb. Negative: may not / might not. Past possibility: may / might + have + past participle.

mistake.why: No -s and no to after may or might.

lessons.summary: Things that are possible but not certain
lessons.title: May and Might
lessons.use: Use may or might for something that is possible. Might often sounds a little less sure than may.

lessons.commonMistake: Had better has no to and is not past: You had better go now, not You had better to go.
lessons.diagramCaption: Strength of advice

examples.sentence: You’d better leave now, or you’ll miss the train.

exercises.prompt: You ___ see a dentist about that tooth.

exercises.explanation: had better + base verb, no to.
exercises.prompt: You ___ hurry, or you’ll miss the train.
You ___ eat so much sugar. It’s bad for you.

lessons.form: should / ought to / had better + base verb. Negative: shouldn’t, ought not to, had better not.

mistake.why: Had better is followed by the base verb, without to.
mistake.wrong: You had better to go now.

lessons.title: Should, Ought to and Had Better
lessons.use: Use should or ought to for advice. Use had better for strong advice when something bad may happen otherwise.

lessons.commonMistake: Use have + participle after the modal: might have gone, not might went.
lessons.diagramCaption: Present evidence supports a conclusion about the past

examples.sentence: The floor is wet; it must have rained.
She might have missed the bus.
They can’t have left yet; their car is here.

exercises.explanation: must have + past participle for a past conclusion.
exercises.prompt: The ground is wet. It ___ rained.

exercises.explanation: can’t have = sure it didn’t happen.
exercises.prompt: He ___ have left yet. His coat is here.
She ___ have missed the bus, but I don’t know.

lessons.form: must/might/could/can’t + have + past participle.

mistake.why: After a modal, use have + past participle for the past.

lessons.title: Deductions about the past
lessons.use: Use modal perfect forms to judge an earlier event from evidence you have now.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not use a before an uncountable noun: say some advice, not an advice.
lessons.diagramCaption: Countable nouns take numbers; uncountable nouns name amounts

examples.meaning: Rice is treated as an amount

exercises.prompt: There aren’t many ___ in the bag.

lessons.form: a/an + singular countable noun · some + plural or uncountable noun.

mistake.why: Advice is uncountable, so it takes no a/an and has no plural.

lessons.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
lessons.use: Countable nouns can have a singular and plural form. Uncountable nouns are normally treated as a mass.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not use an apostrophe for an ordinary plural: books, not book’s.
lessons.diagramCaption: Plural -s and possessive apostrophes do different jobs

exercises.explanation: Child has an irregular plural: children.
exercises.prompt: There are two ___ in the garden.
The ___ toys are on the floor.

lessons.form: one book → two books · child → children · Sara’s book · the students’ books.

mistake.why: An ordinary plural takes no apostrophe.

lessons.summary: More than one, and who owns it
lessons.title: Plurals and possessive ’s
lessons.use: Use plural forms for more than one; use possessive ’s to connect a person or animal to something they have.

lessons.commonMistake: Choose a or an by sound: an hour, a university.
lessons.diagramCaption: A new thing becomes the known thing

examples.meaning: One dog, introduced for the first time

exercises.prompt: I saw ___ elephant at the zoo.

exercises.explanation: A job with a vowel sound: an.
First mention: an. Second mention: the.
exercises.prompt: I have ___ umbrella. ___ umbrella is red.

lessons.form: a + consonant sound · an + vowel sound · the + specific noun.

mistake.why: Choose a or an by the sound, and hour starts with a vowel sound.

lessons.title: A, an, and the
lessons.use: Use a/an for one non-specific countable thing; use the for something specific or already known.

lessons.commonMistake: Match number: these books, not this books.
lessons.diagramCaption: Distance and number determine the demonstrative

exercises.prompt: Who are ___ people next to you?

lessons.form: this/that + singular noun · these/those + plural noun.

mistake.why: Match number: this/that with singular, these/those with plural.

lessons.summary: Pointing to near and far things
lessons.title: This, that, these, and those
lessons.use: Use this/these for something near the speaker and that/those for something farther away.

lessons.commonMistake: Use I as the subject and me as the object: He helped me.
lessons.diagramCaption: Subject, action, and object occupy different positions

examples.meaning: She acts; me receives the call

exercises.prompt: ___ is my brother. He lives in Rome.

exercises.explanation: them is the object form of they.

lessons.form: I/me · he/him · she/her · we/us · they/them.

mistake.why: Use I as the subject and me as the object.

lessons.summary: Who acts and who receives an action
lessons.title: Subject and object pronouns
lessons.use: A subject pronoun usually comes before the verb; an object pronoun follows a verb or preposition.

lessons.commonMistake: Don’t use any in a simple positive sentence: I have any money is wrong. Say I have some money.
lessons.diagramCaption: Where each word fits

examples.sentence: I have some friends in Paris.

exercises.prompt: Is there ___ milk in the fridge?

lessons.form: some + plural or uncountable noun · any + plural or uncountable noun. Any can also mean “it doesn’t matter which”.

mistake.why: Any is used in negatives and questions, some in positive statements.

lessons.summary: Unspecified amounts in statements, questions, and negatives
lessons.title: Some and Any
lessons.use: Use some in positive sentences and in offers or requests. Use any in negatives and most questions.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not add the before a general plural: Dogs need exercise.
lessons.diagramCaption: The narrows a general idea to a known one

examples.sentence: The music next door is loud.

exercises.explanation: General plural or uncountable nouns need no article.
School as an institution: no article.
exercises.prompt: She goes to ___ school by bus.

lessons.form: Books are useful. · The books on this shelf are mine.

mistake.why: Do not add the before a general plural.

lessons.title: The or no article
lessons.use: Leave out an article when speaking generally about plural or uncountable nouns; use the when a specific group or item is clear.

lessons.commonMistake: Use many with countable plurals and much with uncountable nouns.
lessons.diagramCaption: Quantity words depend on countability

examples.sentence: There are a few seats left.

exercises.prompt: How ___ people came to the party?
There are ___ eggs left. We can make an omelette.

lessons.form: many/few + plural countable · much/little + uncountable · some/any + either type.

mistake.why: Many goes with countable plurals; much goes with uncountable nouns.

lessons.summary: Some, any, much, many, few, and little
lessons.title: Quantifiers
lessons.use: Choose quantity words according to whether the noun is countable and how much is meant.

lessons.commonMistake: A possessive pronoun stands alone: mine, not mine book.
lessons.diagramCaption: One form shows ownership; another points back to the subject

examples.meaning: He and himself refer to one person

exercises.explanation: Mine stands alone, without a noun.
Subject and object are the same person: herself.

lessons.form: my book → mine · her book → hers · she → herself.

mistake.why: Mine stands alone; before a noun, use my.

lessons.summary: Ownership and action back to the subject
lessons.title: Possessive and reflexive pronouns
lessons.use: Use possessive forms to show who owns something and reflexive forms when the object refers back to the subject.

lessons.commonMistake: Avoid a second negative in standard English: I didn’t see anyone, not I didn’t see nobody.
lessons.diagramCaption: Prefixes change how definite the reference is

examples.sentence: Someone left a note for you.

examples.meaning: Any person in a negative sentence

exercises.prompt: I didn’t see ___ at the shop.
There is ___ in the box. It’s empty.

lessons.form: some-/any-/no-/every- + one/body/thing/where.

mistake.why: Standard English avoids a second negative.

lessons.title: Indefinite pronouns
lessons.use: Use these pronouns when a person or thing is not named or not known.

lessons.commonMistake: Every takes a singular verb: Every student are late is wrong. Say Every student is late.

labels: three or more: all, every, each

lessons.diagramCaption: How many are you talking about?

exercises.prompt: ___ student in the class has a laptop.
I have two sisters. ___ of them live in Paris.
I don’t like ___ of the two films.

lessons.form: all + plural · every / each + singular noun and singular verb · both + plural · either / neither + singular noun.

mistake.why: Every takes a singular verb.

lessons.summary: Words for whole groups and pairs
lessons.title: All, Every, Each, Both, Either, Neither
lessons.use: All, every, and each talk about three or more. Both, either, and neither talk about exactly two.

lessons.commonMistake: The modifier normally stays singular: shoe shop, not shoes shop.
lessons.diagramCaption: The last noun is the head; earlier nouns narrow its meaning

examples.meaning: The plan is the main noun

exercises.explanation: A noun used as a modifier is singular.
In compounds, the number noun stays singular.
The modifying noun comes first: coffee cup.

lessons.form: modifier noun + head noun; a longer phrase may contain several modifiers.

mistake.why: A noun used as a modifier stays singular.

lessons.title: Noun modifiers
lessons.use: Put a noun before another noun to classify it; the final noun names the main thing.

lessons.commonMistake: I am boring means I make others bored; use I am bored for your feeling.
lessons.diagramCaption: The -ing thing causes the -ed feeling

exercises.explanation: -ing describes the thing that causes the feeling.

exercises.prompt: I felt ___ after the long walk.

exercises.explanation: The news causes the feeling: shocking.

lessons.form: interested person · interesting subject.

mistake.right: I am bored in this class.
mistake.why: -ing describes what causes the feeling; -ed describes the person feeling it.
mistake.wrong: I am boring in this class.

lessons.summary: A feeling or what causes it
lessons.title: -ed and -ing adjectives
lessons.use: Use -ed to describe how someone feels and -ing to describe the thing that produces that feeling.

lessons.commonMistake: With be, put a frequency adverb after be: She is often late.
lessons.diagramCaption: Different adverbs answer different questions

exercises.explanation: hard is both an adjective and an adverb.
often is a frequency adverb with no -ly form.

lessons.form: verb + manner adverb · frequency adverb before a main verb, but after be.

mistake.why: A frequency adverb goes after be.

lessons.title: Adverbs of manner and frequency
lessons.use: Manner adverbs describe an action; frequency adverbs say how regularly it happens.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not double the comparison: more easier is wrong; easier is enough.
lessons.diagramCaption: Comparison form depends on what is being compared

examples.sentence: This route is shorter than the old one.
It is the quietest room here.

exercises.prompt: This bag is ___ than that one.
She is the ___ student in class.
This book is ___ than the film.
He is as tall ___ his brother.

lessons.form: -er / more + adjective + than · the -est / the most + adjective · as + adjective + as.

mistake.why: Do not double the comparison.

lessons.title: Comparatives and superlatives
lessons.use: Use a comparative for two things and a superlative to identify one at an extreme within a group.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not force a long adjective chain; two clear adjectives often sound more natural.
lessons.diagramCaption: Typical adjective order moves from opinion toward type

examples.sentence: She found a beautiful old wooden table.
He bought a small blue bag.

lessons.form: opinion → size → age → colour → origin/material → noun.

mistake.why: Opinion comes before colour.

lessons.title: Adjective order
lessons.use: When several adjectives come before a noun, opinion usually comes before size, age, colour, origin, and material.

lessons.commonMistake: Enough follows an adjective but precedes a noun: warm enough; enough space.
lessons.diagramCaption: Enough marks a useful threshold; too goes beyond it

examples.sentence: The tea is too hot to drink.

exercises.prompt: The soup is ___ hot. I can’t eat it.
The room isn’t big ___ for ten people.
I’m ___ tired. I think I’ll go to bed.

lessons.form: very + adjective · too + adjective · adjective + enough · enough + noun.

mistake.why: Enough goes before a noun but after an adjective.

lessons.title: Degree, too, and enough
lessons.use: Use intensifiers to change degree, too for more than is acceptable, and enough for a sufficient amount.

lessons.commonMistake: Don’t say so a long film. Use such a long film.
lessons.diagramCaption: Adjective or noun?

examples.sentence: It was such a long film.
It was so cold that we stayed in.

exercises.prompt: He speaks ___ quickly that I can’t follow.

lessons.form: so + adjective / adverb · such + (a/an) + (adjective) + noun. Add that to show a result.

mistake.right: It was such a long film.
mistake.why: Use such before a noun phrase, so before an adjective alone.
mistake.wrong: It was so a long film.

lessons.title: So and Such
lessons.use: Use so before an adjective or adverb. Use such before a noun, with or without an adjective before it.

lessons.commonMistake: Say on the table for something resting on its surface.
lessons.diagramCaption: The ball is in, on, or under the box

examples.sentence: The ball is in the box.
The ball is on the box.
The ball is under the box.

exercises.explanation: at for a point or place.
exercises.prompt: I’ll meet you ___ the bus stop.
The shoes are ___ the bed, not on it.

lessons.form: preposition + place or object.

mistake.right: The book is on the table.
mistake.why: On is for something resting on a surface.
mistake.wrong: The book is in the table.

lessons.title: Prepositions of place
lessons.use: In means inside; on means touching a surface; under means below something.

lessons.commonMistake: Say in the morning, but at night.
lessons.diagramCaption: At points to a time, on to a day, and in to a longer period

exercises.prompt: I wake up early ___ the morning.

lessons.form: at + time · on + day/date · in + month/year/season.

mistake.why: Say in the morning but at night.

lessons.title: Prepositions of time
lessons.use: Use at for a clock time, on for a day or date, and in for a month, year, season, or long period.

lessons.commonMistake: Use in for position and into for movement toward the inside.
lessons.diagramCaption: Into describes a change of position

examples.meaning: Movement from one side to the other

exercises.explanation: over = from one side to the other.
through = inside from one side to the other.

lessons.form: move + to a destination · into a space · onto a surface · through an interior · across an area.

mistake.why: Into shows movement toward the inside; in shows position.

lessons.summary: To, into, onto, through, and across
lessons.title: Prepositions of movement
lessons.use: Choose a preposition that shows the direction or path of movement.

lessons.commonMistake: Don’t say arrive to: I arrived to the airport is wrong. Say I arrived at the airport.
lessons.diagramCaption: Choose by the kind of place

exercises.prompt: We arrived ___ the airport at noon.

lessons.form: go / come / return to + place · arrive in + city / country · arrive at + station / airport / hotel · get to + place.

mistake.why: Arrive is followed by at or in, not to.

lessons.title: Go to, Arrive at, Arrive in
lessons.use: Use to after verbs of movement. Use arrive in for towns and countries, and arrive at for smaller places and points.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not translate the preposition word for word from another language.
lessons.diagramCaption: The main word selects its usual preposition

examples.sentence: The result depends on the weather.

lessons.form: interested in · depend on · listen to · proud of.

mistake.why: Many adjectives and verbs need a fixed preposition; learn them together.

lessons.summary: Words that regularly pair with a preposition
lessons.title: Dependent prepositions
lessons.use: Many adjectives and verbs take a particular preposition. Learn the pair as one phrase.

lessons.commonMistake: Don’t use until for a deadline: I must finish until Friday is wrong. Say by Friday.
lessons.diagramCaption: Deadline or duration

exercises.prompt: Please send the report ___ Friday. It’s the deadline.

lessons.form: by + time (send it by Friday) · until + time (wait until Friday).

mistake.why: By is a deadline; until is how long something continues.

lessons.summary: A deadline or a time something continues
lessons.title: By and Until
lessons.use: Use by for a deadline: no later than that time. Use until (or till) for something that continues up to that time.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not normally omit a subject in an English statement: It is raining.
lessons.diagramCaption: A basic English statement moves from subject to verb to object

exercises.explanation: Time expressions often go at the end.

lessons.form: subject + verb + object/complement.

mistake.why: English statements normally need a subject.

lessons.title: Basic word order
lessons.use: In a basic statement, say who or what acts, then the action, then its object if there is one.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not use do with have got: Have you got a pen?
lessons.diagramCaption: Be and have got answer different questions

exercises.explanation: Have you got…? asks about possession.

lessons.form: I am / she is / they are · I have / she has · I’ve got / she’s got.

mistake.why: Have got forms questions without do.
mistake.wrong: Do you have got a pen?

lessons.title: Be and have got
lessons.use: Use be for identity or state and have/have got for possession. Have got is especially common in conversation.

lessons.commonMistake: Match the verb to what follows: There are two chairs, not there is two chairs.
lessons.diagramCaption: The noun that follows determines is or are

exercises.prompt: There ___ a book on the table.
There ___ three chairs in the room.

lessons.form: there is + singular/uncountable · there are + plural.

mistake.why: The verb agrees with the noun that follows.

lessons.title: There is and there are
lessons.use: Use there is to introduce one thing or an uncountable amount, and there are for plural things.

lessons.commonMistake: After did, use the base verb: Where did she go?, not did she went?
lessons.diagramCaption: Question word and auxiliary come before the main verb

exercises.explanation: Question word + does + subject + base verb.

lessons.form: auxiliary + subject + base verb? · question word + auxiliary + subject + base verb?

mistake.why: After did, use the base verb.

lessons.title: Question forms
lessons.use: Put an auxiliary before the subject in most questions; add a question word when asking for specific information.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not use two finite auxiliaries: She doesn’t can go is wrong; She can’t go is right.
lessons.diagramCaption: The negative attaches to an auxiliary
lessons.form: am/is/are not · do/does/did not + base verb · modal + not + base verb.

mistake.why: Do not combine do with a modal verb.

lessons.summary: Saying that something is not true
lessons.title: Negatives and auxiliaries
lessons.use: Add not to an auxiliary or be. Use do/does/did when a simple-tense statement has no other auxiliary.

lessons.commonMistake: Use a before a singular countable noun after what: What a surprise!
lessons.diagramCaption: Different sentence shapes express instructions and reactions
lessons.form: base verb + rest · don’t + base verb · what + (a/an) + noun! · how + adjective/adverb!

mistake.why: After what, use a before a singular countable noun.

lessons.title: Imperatives and exclamations
lessons.use: Use a base verb for an instruction; use what or how to express a strong reaction.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not match the verb to the nearest noun: The box of pencils is here.
lessons.diagramCaption: The head of the subject controls the verb

examples.sentence: The list of names is long.
The players on the team are ready.

exercises.explanation: News is uncountable and takes a singular verb.
Neither of + noun usually takes a singular verb.

lessons.form: singular subject + singular verb · plural subject + plural verb.

mistake.right: The box of pencils is here.
mistake.why: The verb agrees with the head noun, box, not the nearest noun.
mistake.wrong: The box of pencils are here.

lessons.summary: Matching the verb to the subject
lessons.title: Subject–verb agreement
lessons.use: The verb agrees with the grammatical subject, even if other words appear between them.

lessons.commonMistake: Repeat the matching auxiliary in the tag: He can swim, can’t he?
lessons.diagramCaption: The tag usually reverses the statement’s polarity
lessons.form: positive statement + negative tag · negative statement + positive tag.

mistake.why: The tag repeats the same auxiliary with the opposite polarity.

lessons.title: Question tags
lessons.use: Add a short question after a statement to check information or invite a response.

lessons.commonMistake: Its is possessive; it’s means it is or it has.
lessons.diagramCaption: An apostrophe can change the meaning of it’s

exercises.explanation: It’s = it is, with an apostrophe.

options: I bought eggs, milk and bread.
I bought, eggs milk and bread.
I bought eggs milk, and, bread.

lessons.form: Capital + sentence · ? for a direct question · ’ for possession/contraction.

mistake.why: Its shows possession; it’s means it is or it has.

lessons.title: Capital letters and punctuation
lessons.use: Start a sentence and proper name with a capital letter; use punctuation to mark endings, questions, and possession.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not use for + base verb to express purpose: say to ask, not for ask.
lessons.diagramCaption: The infinitive explains the purpose of the first action

examples.sentence: I called to ask a question.
She went outside to get some air.

exercises.prompt: I went to the shop ___ some milk.

exercises.explanation: stop to do = stop in order to do something.

lessons.form: main action + to + base verb.

mistake.right: I use it to ask questions.
mistake.why: Purpose with a verb uses to + base verb, not for.
mistake.wrong: I use it for ask questions.

lessons.title: Infinitive of purpose
lessons.use: Use to + base verb to explain the purpose of an action.

lessons.commonMistake: Say make a mistake and do homework, not do a mistake or make homework.
lessons.diagramCaption: Activity or product

examples.sentence: I do my homework after school.

exercises.explanation: do a favour is a fixed phrase.

exercises.prompt: I need to ___ a phone call.

lessons.form: do homework / the dishes / a job / your best · make a cake / a mistake / a decision / a phone call.

mistake.why: Mistake goes with make; homework goes with do.

lessons.summary: Two common verbs that are easy to confuse
lessons.title: Do or Make?
lessons.use: Use do for tasks, work, and activities. Use make for creating or producing something and for many fixed phrases.

lessons.commonMistake: Stop doing means end an action; stop to do means pause for another purpose.
lessons.diagramCaption: The first verb determines the next verb form

examples.meaning: He paused another action in order to rest

lessons.form: enjoy + verb-ing · decide + to-infinitive · stop + verb-ing / to-infinitive.

mistake.why: Stop doing ends an action; stop to do pauses for another purpose.
mistake.wrong: He stopped to smoke. (meaning he quit)

lessons.title: -ing forms and infinitives
lessons.use: Some verbs take an -ing form, some take to + verb, and some allow both with a change in meaning.

lessons.commonMistake: Say turn it off, not turn off it. Look after is not separated.
lessons.diagramCaption: Object position depends on the phrasal verb

examples.meaning: Off completes a separable phrasal verb

examples.sentence: Can you look after my cat?

exercises.prompt: Please ___ your shoes before you come in.
The meeting was ___ because of the rain.

lessons.form: turn on the light / turn the light on · turn it on · look after someone.

mistake.why: With a pronoun, put the object between the verb and the particle.

lessons.title: Phrasal verbs
lessons.use: A particle can change a verb’s meaning. With a separable phrasal verb, a pronoun object goes between the verb and particle.

lessons.commonMistake: I’m knowing is not the usual form for a state; say I know.
lessons.diagramCaption: Meaning determines whether a continuous form is natural

examples.meaning: Have means eat here, an action

exercises.explanation: Stative verbs like understand rarely take the continuous.

exercises.prompt: She ___ a new car. She loves it.

exercises.explanation: taste with this meaning is stative.

lessons.form: I know the answer. · I’m thinking about it.

mistake.why: Verbs of state usually avoid the continuous form.

lessons.title: Stative verbs
lessons.use: Verbs of belief, possession, and feeling often describe a state and usually use a simple form; some change meaning in a continuous form.

lessons.commonMistake: After be used to, use -ing: I’m used to get up early is wrong. Say I’m used to getting up early.
lessons.diagramCaption: Past habit or familiar now

examples.sentence: I used to live in Rome.
I’m used to getting up early.
She is getting used to the cold.

exercises.explanation: used to + base verb for a past state.
exercises.prompt: She ___ in a big city, but now she lives in a village.
It took a while to get used to ___ on the left.

lessons.form: used to + base verb · am/is/are used to + verb-ing or noun · get used to + verb-ing or noun.

mistake.right: I’m used to getting up early.
mistake.why: After be used to or get used to, use -ing or a noun.
mistake.wrong: I’m used to get up early.

lessons.title: Used to, Be Used to and Get Used to
lessons.use: Use used to + verb for a past habit that has stopped. Use be used to + -ing for something familiar. Use get used to + -ing for becoming familiar.

lessons.commonMistake: Use despite + noun or -ing, not despite + full clause without the fact that.
lessons.diagramCaption: Linking words tell the reader how ideas relate

examples.sentence: We stayed inside because it was cold.
Although it was cold, we went out.

exercises.prompt: I was tired, ___ I went to bed.
She stayed at home ___ she was ill.
I like tea, ___ I don’t like coffee.

lessons.form: because + clause · so + result clause · although + clause · despite + noun/-ing.

mistake.right: Despite the rain, we went out.
mistake.why: Despite takes a noun or -ing form, not a full clause.
mistake.wrong: Despite it was raining, we went out.

lessons.title: Reason, result, and contrast
lessons.use: Join ideas by showing why something happened, what followed, or how two facts contrast.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not normally use will in the future time clause: when I arrive, not when I will arrive.
lessons.diagramCaption: The time clause places one event before another

examples.meaning: The arrival is in the future

exercises.explanation: Use the present after when for the future.
exercises.prompt: I’ll call you when I ___ home.
Please wait here until she ___ back.

exercises.explanation: Present Simple for future time after as soon as.
exercises.prompt: As soon as we ___ , we’ll have lunch.

lessons.form: when/before/after/until + clause, main clause.

mistake.right: When I arrive, I’ll call you.
mistake.why: Use the present, not will, in a future time clause.
mistake.wrong: When I will arrive, I’ll call you.

lessons.title: Time clauses
lessons.use: Use a time clause to place one event in relation to another. A future meaning normally takes a present verb after when or until.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not put commas around information needed to identify the noun.
lessons.diagramCaption: The relative clause identifies which woman is meant

examples.sentence: The woman who lives upstairs is a nurse.
I found the book that you wanted.

exercises.prompt: The woman ___ lives next door is a doctor.

exercises.explanation: that for things in a defining clause.
exercises.prompt: The book ___ I bought is great.
That is the man ___ car was stolen.

lessons.form: noun + who/which/that + defining clause; no separating commas.

mistake.right: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
mistake.why: No commas around information needed to identify the noun.
mistake.wrong: The man, who lives next door, is a doctor. (more than one man)

lessons.title: Defining relative clauses
lessons.use: Add essential information that identifies the noun. Who refers to people; which to things; that can refer to either in this kind of clause.

lessons.commonMistake: Don’t use but with although: Although it was cold, but we went out is wrong.
lessons.diagramCaption: Contrast or preparation

examples.sentence: Although it was cold, we went out.
Take an umbrella in case it rains.

exercises.prompt: ___ it was raining, we went for a walk.

exercises.explanation: in case = be ready for a possibility.
exercises.prompt: Take your phone ___ you need to call us.
He passed the exam ___ he hadn’t studied much.

lessons.form: although / though / even though + subject + verb · in case + subject + present verb.

mistake.right: Although it was cold, we went out.
mistake.why: Do not use but with although.
mistake.wrong: Although it was cold, but we went out.

lessons.summary: Showing contrast and preparing for a possibility
lessons.title: Although, Though, Even Though and In Case
lessons.use: Use although, though, or even though for a contrast. Use in case for something you do to be ready for a possible problem.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not use that in a non-defining relative clause; use who or which.
lessons.diagramCaption: Commas mark information that can be removed

examples.sentence: My aunt, who lives in Cork, is visiting.
The museum, which opened last year, is free.

exercises.prompt: My brother, ___ lives in Rome, is a chef.

exercises.explanation: which for things in a non-defining clause.
exercises.prompt: London, ___ is the capital, is huge.

options: Tom, who is tall, plays basketball.
The man who is tall plays basketball.
The man that is tall plays basketball.

lessons.form: known noun, who/which/whose + extra clause, rest of sentence.

mistake.right: My sister, who lives in Rome, is a nurse.
mistake.why: Non-defining clauses use who or which, not that.
mistake.wrong: My sister, that lives in Rome, is a nurse.

lessons.title: Non-defining relative clauses
lessons.use: Add information about a noun already identified; the sentence still identifies it if the clause is removed.

lessons.commonMistake: Keep the understood subject clear: Walking home, the café caught my eye wrongly makes the café the walker.
lessons.diagramCaption: The participle clause shares its subject with the main clause

examples.meaning: I was walking and I noticed it
examples.sentence: Walking home, I noticed a new café.
Built in 1900, the bridge still stands.

exercises.explanation: Present participle for an earlier action by the same subject.
exercises.prompt: ___ the news, she called her mother.

exercises.explanation: Past participle has a passive meaning.
exercises.prompt: The book ___ by Orwell is famous.

exercises.explanation: Present participle shows a reason or situation.
exercises.prompt: ___ in Paris, he speaks French well.

lessons.form: verb-ing clause, main clause · past participle clause, main clause.

mistake.right: Walking home, I noticed the café.
mistake.why: The understood subject must be the same as the main subject.
mistake.wrong: Walking home, the café caught my eye.

lessons.title: Participle clauses
lessons.use: Use an -ing or past-participle clause to link related actions or states, usually with the same understood subject as the main clause.

lessons.commonMistake: Keep the tense on be: is built (present), was built (past).
lessons.diagramCaption: The receiver of the action becomes the subject

examples.sentence: The window was broken last night.
The invitations are sent by email.

lessons.form: be in the needed tense + past participle; optional by + actor.

mistake.why: Keep be in the passive, in the right tense.

lessons.summary: Focusing on the action or receiver
lessons.title: The passive voice
lessons.use: Use the passive when the action or its receiver matters more than who did it, or when the actor is unknown.

lessons.commonMistake: When a that-clause follows told, name the listener: She told me that she was tired.
lessons.diagramCaption: A report changes viewpoint from the original speaker

examples.sentence: ‘I’m tired,’ Lea said. → Lea said she was tired.
He told us he had already eaten.

exercises.prompt: “I am tired,” she said. → She said she ___ tired.
“I will help,” he said. → He said he ___ help.
“We live here,” they said. → They said they ___ there.

lessons.form: said (that) + reported clause · told + person + (that) + reported clause.

mistake.right: She told me that she was tired.
mistake.why: Tell needs a listener; say does not.
mistake.wrong: She told that she was tired.

lessons.title: Reported statements
lessons.use: Report another person’s statement. When the reporting verb is in the past, verb forms often shift back if the situation is viewed from that past point.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not keep question inversion: asked where I was, not asked where was I.
lessons.diagramCaption: Reported questions use statement word order

examples.sentence: ‘Where are you?’ → She asked where I was.
‘Please wait.’ → He asked us to wait.

exercises.prompt: “Where do you live?” → She asked where I ___ .
“Close the door.” → He told me ___ the door.

exercises.explanation: Yes/no questions use if or whether.
exercises.prompt: “Are you ready?” → She asked ___ I was ready.

lessons.form: asked + if/whether or question word + subject + verb · told + person + to + verb.

mistake.why: Reported questions use statement word order.

lessons.title: Reported questions and commands
lessons.use: Report a question with statement word order; report an instruction with told/asked + person + to-infinitive.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not drop being from an ongoing passive: is being repaired.
lessons.diagramCaption: The auxiliary pattern changes passive meaning

examples.meaning: A reported claim with passive reporting
examples.sentence: The artist is said to live abroad.

exercises.explanation: Present continuous passive: is being + past participle.
It is said / He is said to…
exercises.prompt: He ___ to be a good teacher.

lessons.form: to be + participle · being + participle · it is said that / subject is said to.

mistake.right: The road is being repaired right now.
mistake.why: An ongoing passive needs being.
mistake.wrong: The road is repaired right now.

lessons.title: Advanced passive forms
lessons.use: Use passive infinitives, continuous forms, and reporting patterns when the action or claim is more important than its actor.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not use one pattern for every reporting verb: deny doing, not deny to do.
lessons.diagramCaption: Each reporting verb selects its own complement pattern
lessons.form: advise + person + to + verb · deny + verb-ing · promise + to + verb · insist + that-clause.

mistake.why: Reporting verbs follow different patterns; deny takes -ing.

lessons.title: Reporting verb patterns
lessons.use: Choose the complement pattern required by the reporting verb; different verbs take a person, an -ing form, an infinitive, or a that-clause.

lessons.commonMistake: Invert the auxiliary, not the main verb: Never have I seen, not Never seen I.
lessons.diagramCaption: Fronting a negative expression moves the auxiliary before the subject

examples.sentence: Never had I heard such silence.
Only later did we understand why.

exercises.explanation: After a negative adverb at the start, invert auxiliary and subject.

exercises.prompt: Not only ___ late, but he also forgot the tickets.

lessons.form: negative adverbial + auxiliary + subject + main verb.

mistake.why: After a negative adverb at the start, invert the auxiliary and the subject.

lessons.summary: Formal emphasis with reversed word order
lessons.title: Inversion after negative adverbials
lessons.use: Place a negative or restrictive adverbial first to add emphasis, then put the auxiliary before the subject.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not keep if after inversion: Had I known, not If had I known.
lessons.diagramCaption: Formal inversion replaces if in the condition

examples.sentence: Had I known, I would have called.
Should you need help, contact us.

exercises.explanation: Had I known = If I had known.
exercises.prompt: ___ I known, I would have helped.

exercises.explanation: Should you need = If you need.
Were I you = If I were you.

lessons.form: Had + subject + participle · Were + subject + complement/to-infinitive · Should + subject + base verb.

mistake.right: Had I known, I’d have called.
mistake.why: Inversion replaces if; do not keep both.
mistake.wrong: If had I known, I’d have called.

lessons.title: Inversion in conditionals
lessons.use: In formal style, omit if and put had, were, or should before the subject.

lessons.commonMistake: Do not add a second subject: It was Nia who found it, not It was Nia who she found it.
lessons.diagramCaption: A cleft sentence places one element in focus

examples.sentence: It was Nia who found the key.

examples.meaning: A quiet hour is the focus
examples.sentence: What I need is a quiet hour.

exercises.prompt: The thing ___ annoys me is the noise.

lessons.form: It is/was + focus + that/who + clause · What + clause + is/was + focus.

mistake.right: It was Nia who found it.
mistake.why: Who already acts as the subject, so do not add another.
mistake.wrong: It was Nia who she found it.

lessons.title: Cleft sentences
lessons.use: Use a cleft structure to highlight a person, time, place, or reason rather than present every part equally.

lessons.commonMistake: Only omit words when the listener can identify what is missing.
lessons.diagramCaption: A shorter form points back to a known idea

examples.sentence: I ordered tea, and Noor did too.
Need a charger? I have one.

exercises.explanation: The auxiliary replaces the whole verb phrase.

exercises.prompt: I don’t like this shirt. I’ll buy the red ___ .

exercises.explanation: So + auxiliary + subject agrees with a positive statement.

lessons.form: full idea → recoverable gap or substitute word.

mistake.why: Use an auxiliary to stand in for the omitted verb phrase.

lessons.title: Ellipsis and substitution
lessons.use: Omit words that are clear from context or replace them with a short form such as one, so, or an auxiliary.

lessons.commonMistake: The past form does not mean past time here; it shows distance from the current reality.
lessons.diagramCaption: A past form can express an unreal present preference

examples.meaning: I prefer you to stay now

exercises.explanation: It’s time + past form for a present or future need.
would rather + past for a preference about someone else.
as if + past shows an unreal comparison.
exercises.prompt: He talks as if he ___ everything.

lessons.form: It’s time + subject + past simple · I’d rather + subject + past simple.

mistake.why: The past form shows distance from reality, not past time.

lessons.summary: Past forms for present wishes and preferences
lessons.title: Unreal time
lessons.use: Use a past form after expressions such as it’s time or I’d rather to show that the idea is unreal, preferred, or overdue now.
